title: I wanted an iPod for my kids. I found this device instead.
summary: For kids too young for a phone, a music player that can do Spotify or Apple Music — and doesn't have an internet browser — is tricky.
content: The Globluum music player is slightly larger than a cassette, and great for kids and tweens. Katie Notopoulos / Business Insider Parents are looking for a music player for their kids who aren't old enough for a phone. My goal: something that can stream Spotify, Amazon, and Apple music, but doesn't have an internet browser or other apps. I recommend this $70 music player for tweens and kids! The children of today (ok, maybe their parents) yearn for an old iPod . Something I've heard over and over, both in real conversations with mom friends and in online parenting groups, is the desire to have some form of kid-friendly music player. Something like an iPod, if Apple hadn't discontinued them . I've found the solution: it's this $70 music player from Globluum . The Globluum music player for kids can offline sync Spotify, Amazon Music, and Apple Music, but has no apps or internet access. Amazon There's a new tricky age for kids when they're too old for the baby-ish Fisher Price-type versions of technology, but too young for their own phone. There are some great screen-free audio devices — the Toniebox or the Yoto player , but these are generally designed for preschoolers and young kids. The problem is with those upper-elementary and middle-school kids — let's say ages 7 to 13 — who want to listen to real adult music, not Kidz Bop or "Baby Shark." This is a crucial and formative time for kids to develop their own musical taste, and connect with peers and culture through music. If you're over 35, you probably remember buying your first CDs or cassettes at Sam Goody or Borders around this age. Maybe you even taped songs off the radio. There's a good chance that videos popular on MTV when you were 11 are still burned into your brain. But things are different now. Most people, both young and old, listen to music through a streaming app like Spotify or Apple Music, or through YouTube. And while there are good options for this at home (or hey, even a record player!), the trick is a portable player for kids when they leave the house. This was exactly my son's problem. He loved listening to music on his iPad at home, but he wanted something small he could fit in his pocket on the go. At 10, he's old enough to have his own musical taste, but too young for a phone. Here was what I was looking for in a device: No text, calling, or internet browser No games or other apps, just music Bluetooth for headphones and a built-in speaker Apple Music and Spotify compatible Can offline sync playlists so it can be played when not streaming on WiFi Doesn't need to be connected to a computer or use a cord Some form of parental controls Pocket-sized and portable I have a feeling this is the list of requirements you're looking for, too. In a twist that was shocking to me, I found that Amazon's AI assistant was actually really helpful to sort through the various options when I searched for "music player for kids." There are a lot of options and various price points from brands you've never heard, and it was hard to tell what features each one had without combing through the listings in detail. The AI assistant helped in a low-information environment like that. The Globluum in an adult's hand (my son does not actually listen to Bob Seger, at least not willingly). Katie Notopoulos / Business Insider That's how I ended up with the Globluum MP3 player for kids. And now, dear friend (we're friends now, aren't we?), I'm recommending it to you. To be clear, there's some downsides: Battery life isn't great. Its listing says 25 hours of playtime, but it definitely runs down faster if you have the screen on. The operating system is slow and laggy. This isn't a $1,000 iPhone! The weird "kid-friendly" design of the apps is kind of uncool and a tween probably wishes it just looked like normal app logos instead of something babyish. Is this the greatest device ever? Absolutely not. No offense to the fine folks at Globluum (hilarious name), but it definitely feels cheap and sort of crappy. But its job is to do one thing (play music) and it does that one thing. At around $70, the price point was about as high as I wanted to go for this kind of device, especially since I suspect there's a high risk of it getting lost or damaged. Anyway, I solved this problem for you! Enjoy!!!! Read the original article on Business Insider

title: From Waymo to Jeff Bezos' Prometheus, meet the biggest fundraisers in robotics and physical AI
summary: Robotics and physical AI funding hit $97.3 billion so far in 2026, more than double 2025's total.
content: Jeff Bezos Kimberly White/Getty Images for Semafor Robotics and physical AI funding hit $97.3 billion so far in 2026, more than double 2025’s total. Waymo and Jeff Bezos’ Prometheus landed funding rounds of $16 billion and $12 billion, respectively. The boom spans established businesses, defense companies, and early bets on humanoids. From robotaxis and military drones to humanoids that might someday fold your laundry , Silicon Valley is betting billions on a future filled with robots. 2026 was a record year for funding. So far, robotics and physical AI companies have raised $97.3 billion dollars across more than 1,200 deals globally — more than double the $47.4 billion raised in all of 2025, according to Crunchbase. The funding boom spans established businesses like Waymo and early bets on humanoids from companies like Neura Robotics . Defense companies, particularly drone makers such as Anduril, Shield AI, Helsing, and Saronic, account for some of the biggest rounds. Gené Teare, a research lead at Crunchbase, told Business Insider that drones attract more capital because the technology is more mature than other experimental areas of robotics. Sanjay Aggarwal, a partner at VC firm F-Prime, pointed to four drivers of the boom: growth in autonomous vehicles and defense, a push to revive domestic manufacturing, bets on "once-in-a-generation" founders like Jeff Bezos and Travis Kalanick, and futuristic technologies like humanoids. Aggarwal expects the first three categories to keep attracting big checks in 2027, while investors scrutinize the fourth more closely. "You can only raise money on the promise of future revenue for so long," he said. Here are the 10 robotics and physical AI companies that have raised the most funding this year, according to data from Crunchbase. 1. Waymo: $16 billion Waymos in Santa Monica Genaro Molina/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Waymo landed the sector's biggest round of the year so far, and its robots are hard to miss. Its Jaguar robotaxis and new Ojai vehicles trundle along practically every block in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Phoenix. It operates in 15 US cities , with more planned for 2027. Its $16 billion Series D, announced in February, valued Waymo at $126 billion. Dragoneer Investment Group, DST Global, and Sequoia Capital led the round, with backing from Alphabet, its majority investor. 2. Prometheus: $12 billion Jeff Bezos is back in the CEO seat. The Amazon founder co-leads Prometheus with former Google X executive Vik Bajaj, marking his first CEO role since leaving Amazon in 2021. The company is building an "artificial general engineer" — AI to help engineers develop and test products from smartphones to jet engines in computer simulations — before manufacturing them in the real world. Its $12 billion Series B, announced in June, valued the company at roughly $41 billion. Investors included Bezos himself, JPMorgan, BlackRock, and Goldman Sachs. 3. Anduril Industries: $5 billion Palmer Luckey Adam Gray/Getty Images for The New York Times Palmer Luckey cofounded his defense tech company nearly a decade ago to build machines for the battlefield. Today, its surveillance towers are deployed along the US-Mexico border, and the company says it has delivered hundreds of Altius drones to Ukrainian forces. The company said it brought in $2.2 billion in revenue last year, more than double its 2024 revenue. Its $5 billion Series H, announced in May, doubled its valuation to $61 billion. Andreessen Horowitz and Thrive Capital led the round. 4. Shield AI: $4 billion Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI builds military drones and Hivemind, an AI pilot for aircraft. Its V-BAT surveillance drone takes off vertically and can fly even in the presence of signal jamming. It helped the US Coast Guard seize $362 million worth of cocaine last year and flew more than 200 missions in Ukraine in 2025. This year, Shield AI raised two $2 billion rounds of financing. In March, the company raised a Series G round led by Advent International and JPMorgan Chase. In November, it announced plans to raise another $2 billion from investors to help fund the acquisition of radar maker Echodyne. The package includes a $1 billion Series H valuing Shield AI at $28.8 billion, plus a separate $1 billion equity investment from Blackstone-managed funds. 5. Zipline International: $2.3 billion Zipline drone Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Zipline began delivering blood in Rwanda in 2016. Today, its drones carry everything from medical supplies to takeout. The company says it has made more than a million deliveries in Dallas-Fort Worth alone this year and is working with Walmart to add 300 delivery sites across the US. Its $1.5 billion Series I, announced this month, valued Zipline at $21.5 billion. Paradigm, WCM Investment Management, and Layer Global led the round. That followed an $800 million Series H that closed in March. 6. Helsing: $1.8 billion Munich-based defense tech company Helsing builds AI software and hardware for military and national security use, including drones and autonomous underwater vehicles. Its HX-2 drone uses AI to navigate and identify targets even when GPS signals are jammed. The company said thousands had been deployed to Ukrainian forces in the first half of 2026 . Its $1.8 billion Series E, announced in July , valued the company at $18 billion. Investors included Dragoneer Investment Group, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and ICONIQ Capital. 7. Saronic: $1.75 billion Austin-based Saronic builds boats designed to operate without crews for the US military and its allies. In June, one of its drone boats, operated by the US Navy, helped rescue two American soldiers after Iran shot down their helicopter off the coast of Oman. The company's $1.75 billion Series D, announced in March , valued it at $9.25 billion. Kleiner Perkins led the round. 8. Atoms: $1.7 billion Travis Kalanick Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images Uber cofounder Travis Kalanick publicly unveiled Atoms earlier this year after years of operating in stealth. The Los Angeles-based company has revealed few details but says it is building robots for food, mining, and transportation. It also absorbed Kalanick's ghost-kitchen business, CloudKitchens , as a subsidiary. Atoms announced a $1.7 billion funding round on July 22, led by Andreessen Horowitz, to pursue what Kalanick called "a journey to digitize the physical world." 9. Skild AI: $1.4 billion Founded by Carnegie Mellon researchers Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta, Pittsburgh-based Skild AI is building an AI model capable of controlling machines ranging from robotic arms to humanoids. Its model is designed to help different robots learn new jobs without being programmed for each task. Skild said in September that it had reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue from more than 60 customers. Projects include robotic assembly with Nvidia and Foxconn and kitchen pilots with Mitsui. Its $1.4 billion Series C, announced on January 14, valued Skild at more than $14 billion. SoftBank Group led the round. 10. Neura Robotics: $1.4 billion Neura Robotics Sven Hoppe/picture alliance via Getty Images Germany's Neura Robotics builds robotic arms and mobile carts and is developing humanoids. Customers can rent space at its "robot gyms" — training centers equipped with simulators and tracking technology — to teach machines specific jobs, then transfer those skills to other robots. Its $1.4 billion Series C, announced in June, was led by Tether Investments, with backing from Amazon, Nvidia, and Bosch. Have a tip? title: He chose culinary school in New York over a master's in engineering. Now he runs his own restaurant in China.
summary: Zhu Guanlin's parents were shocked when he chose culinary school in New York over a master's in engineering. They didn't see being a chef as a stable career path.
content: Zhu Guanlin studied at a culinary school in the US, but when it was time to open his own restaurant, he chose China. Provided by Zhu Guanlin Zhu Guanlin, now 32, came from a family of engineers, but chose to attend culinary school in the US. He worked at Michelin-starred restaurants in New York and San Francisco before moving back to China. In 2025, he opened his own restaurant in Dali, a city in southwestern China. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Zhu Guanlin, 32, head chef and owner of Plum, a restaurant in Dali, China. It has been edited for length and clarity. During my final year studying engineering in China , I was in a constant state of anxiety as I prepared to pursue a master's degree. Near where I lived was a small morning market by the river. In China, the northeast is cold, so all the seafood and freshwater fish were laid out in the open, frozen solid. There were freshly slaughtered pigs, and steam still rising from the meat. As people gathered for breakfast, I'd smell deep-fried foods mixing with the scent of bean-flour flatbreads. The air felt alive with the warmth of daily life. It wasn't just the act of cooking that I loved, but the stories behind the food. Why do people in Sichuan eat spicy food , for instance? It's because of the humidity. I realized that by becoming a chef, I could learn it all. Breaking away I was 21 when I received two acceptance letters: one to study electrical engineering at a university in Virginia, and the other from the Culinary Institute of America. Going back to my grandfather's generation, everyone in my family had been an electrical engineer. I was the first to break away from that path. My decision to go to culinary school was a shock to my parents. I hadn't told them that I'd applied. The idea of being a chef felt foreign to them, and they didn't consider it a stable career. Do you have any regrets about a move abroad ? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. I moved to New York City in 2019 for a two-year associate degree program. My tuition was nearly $40,000 a year. My parents paid for the first year, but I didn't want to continue taking money from them. I started working, and with the help of a scholarship, I paid for the rest of my time abroad myself. He got internships at Michelin-starred restaurants through Curricular Practical Training, a work authorization available to some international students on F-1 visas. Provided by Zhu Guanlin My school is often called the West Point of the culinary world I met a lot of classmates who were retired Special Forces soldiers or Army infantrymen. We joked that we could only use three phrases: "Yes, Chef," "No, Chef," and "I will do better, Chef." The school allowed internships through Curricular Practical Training (CPT), so I was able to work legally in the US . After finishing two semesters, I spent the third working in restaurants, taking on multiple jobs. After graduating, I did stints at various Michelin-starred restaurants, first in New York and later in San Francisco. During my time in the US, the highest position I reached was chef de partie, the supervisor of a specific station. He moved to Dali, a city in southwestern China's Yunnan province, to help a former classmate. Provided by Zhu Guanlin My OPT visa was set to expire in about six months I also realized that unless I became a sous chef or chef de cuisine, I wouldn't grow professionally. After seeing the realities up close, Michelin restaurants also lost their aura of mystique. The things I truly cared about, like the culture behind cuisine, were rooted in China . At the end of 2023, a classmate of mine opened a restaurant in Dali, a city in southwestern China's Yunnan province, and I went to help co-manage it. Business was quiet at first, but after about six months, it took off. But I wanted to open a restaurant of my own, so I left. In February 2025, I opened Plum in Dali, investing 400,000 Chinese yuan, or about $60,000. The restaurant is set in a courtyard, and we have 35 seats in total. The team has grown from four to 10 employees. We don't define ourselves as either Chinese or Western. A single dish might combine Western components, Chinese techniques , and Japanese or Italian influences. I've made a focaccia that incorporates a French-style sauce, then topped it with sautéed porcini mushrooms, Chinese-style. Lately we've been fully booked every day. Based on my current calculations, it'll take about four or five years to break even. In February 2025, Zhu opened Plum, his own restaurant in Dali, China. Provided by Zhu Guanlin Making peace with my parents My parents have realized that being an engineer isn't the only career path. I realize now that back then they were afraid I'd have a hard life. Once I understood that, communicating with them became more relaxed. They even helped fund my new restaurant. New York City was the most diverse city I've ever lived in, where you can find the culture of virtually every ethnic group. That's something I miss. I don't miss some of the Michelin restaurants, though. Sometimes, it felt like they were trying to force a narrative onto their menus. In China, I find kitchen culture can sometimes be cliquey. The master-apprentice system is still dominant, and people can sometimes form groups based on clan ties or local culture, rather than welcome newcomers. I'm still exploring what kitchen culture should look like. Restaurant staff in China typically get four days off a month. I give everyone two consecutive days off each week, plus compensatory time off for holidays. When chefs are overworked, they lose focus. The atmosphere was quiet and orderly at school in New York and in many of the Michelin-starred kitchens I worked at. When I first returned to China , I demanded the same from my own staff. But then, at one point, I realized that it wasn't necessary. When people feel a sense of cohesion and genuine appreciation for their work, they naturally take initiative. title: NAPA's solution to America's blue-collar worker shortage: Make training feel like Madden Football
summary: A former "Madden" producer helped developed tech that NAPA thinks could help America's auto tech shortage.
content: NAPA thinks it's found a tech solution that will accelerate the auto tech talent pipeline. NAPA A former "Madden" producer helped NAPA produce its XR goggles and smart glasses. The technology, NAPA hopes, will help build a pipeline of auto tech talent. The training goggles won a SEMA award as shops contend with a technician shortage. NAPA's auto-repair training is taking a page out of "Madden's" book. The auto-parts company has spent the past two-and-a-half years developing a new training platform, called XcceleratoR, with Robin Cowie, the founder and CEO of Skillmaker. XcceleratoR has two core tech products: XR training goggles that place car-fixers inside a virtual shop with a digital pickup and EV, and smart glasses designed to provide repair guidance as they work on real cars. On paper, Cowie looks like a strange talent to call on amid the auto industry's labor problems . He produced the 1999 hit "The Blair Witch Project" and worked for three years as the senior narrative producer for the "Madden NFL" franchise. He says he helped develop tech with some surprising overlap. "Madden is really a football simulator. A lot of professional players play it, a lot of coaches play it, they teach strategy," he said. "What we've created here is a simulation for technicians." The gamified training blitz comes as repair shops face increasingly difficult tasks: finding and training car mechanics with the skills to work on modern vehicles — and then retaining them. NAPA estimates that the US is short roughly 642,000 technicians. A recent study commissioned by Ford says that each year, 66,000 new technician and mechanic jobs open. "With the amount of jobs and people that want technicians in their shop, and the shortage we have, the first thing we've got to worry about is keeping them," Shawn Gilfillan, the owner of New Jersey-based Automotive Magic repair shops, told Business Insider. Gilfillan's shops use NAPA tools. Inside the tech A technician-in-training uses NAPA's XR glasses. NAPA When technicians first put on the goggles, they start next to a virtual tool bin. Connected handle attachments provide haptic feedback as users tighten nuts and bolts. "The physics have to be real, the tools have to be real, the information has to be real," Cowie said about the VR experience. "If you get the wrong piece of information, you don't fix the car." NAPA says the goggles include 53 lessons, 148 hours of training, and preparation for three Automotive Service Excellence certifications. It says trainees can go from "onboarding to billable" in 25 days. The company also says shops can use a 45- to 60-minute goggle-based assessment to gauge a prospective hire's existing competency. The XR Training Goggles won SEMA's 2026 New Product Award for Emerging Technology Product earlier this month. NAPA said the software had exited beta right before the Vegas auto industry conference. The other half of XcceleratoR is designed for the workday. NAPA's smart glasses use voice commands and vehicle-specific repair information to guide technicians through a job without requiring them to repeatedly leave their workstation for a computer terminal. The system draws on NAPA's own knowledge base and repair information from partners including Identifix and AutoVitals. The premise is that their familiar, game-like software could help a fresh batch of technicians build their skills faster — and without forcing them to read the nearly 1,900-page books that trained the old generation of car-fixers. Once the new talent is trained, the glasses can help keep the repair shop flowing. " Cars are extremely complicated . They're rolling computers," Jason Rainey, NAPA's vice president of commercial sales, said. "Now you're taking the actual systems that they were gaming with and using that to apply in a skill set that will last in the next 40 years." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Former Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson, 59, says his athletic experience helped him through stroke rehab
summary: Four-time Olympic gold medalist Michael Johnson, 59, shared what kept him going through difficult weeks of stroke rehab.
content: Former Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson says focusing on small gains helped him through stroke rehab. David Madison/Getty Images Former sprinter Michael Johnson says his athletic mindset helped him recover from a stroke. Years of Olympic training helped him spot progress in his recovery that he might otherwise have missed. He said that gave him a reason to keep going when he felt he wasn't getting better. Former Olympic sprinter Michael Johnson, 59, says his mindset as an athlete helped him through stroke rehab . On Wednesday's episode of the " How to Fail with Elizabeth Day " podcast, the four-time Olympic gold medalist spoke about suffering a stroke in 2018, which left him unable to walk and with limited movement in his left arm and fingers. "The rehabilitation was hard, but it was much easier for me because of having been an Olympic athlete," Johnson said. "So many stroke survivors don't make a full recovery or don't make as much of a recovery as they can, because they stop short and they give up," Johnson said. "Because they don't recognize what I was very fortunate to have experience in recognizing — which is how you actually train for these tiny marginal gains every day." Johnson said years of training for small improvements helped him notice daily progress in his recovery that others might have missed. His past athletic training also helped him through weeks when he felt his recovery had stalled. He remembered the same frustration from preparing for the Olympics , when hard work didn't always produce noticeable results. "I know, though, that I got better, and that is the motivation that keeps you going," he added. Johnson said the stroke recovery process was physically demanding and could be disheartening. "When you see that I am a shell of what I used to be in terms of how much weight I can lift, and how much coordination I can have, it's not very uplifting, right?" he said. "But you have to be able to, and that is the same thing again. I had the benefit of having been through it as an athlete." Others have also spoken about the value of small improvements during recovery. Lime CEO Wayne Ting told Business Insider in October that recovering from a stroke, like improving his company's finances, involved getting "1% better" every day. Lessons from sports can carry into other parts of life, too, including work. Goldman Sachs executive and former college lacrosse player Madison Crutchfield told Business Insider in October 2025 that competing taught her to stay levelheaded under pressure and respond constructively when things went wrong. title: 42 state attorneys want to stop Character.ai from auctioning private chat histories to the highest bidder
summary: State attorneys general said that the now-bankrupt AI chatbot company is planning to sell chat histories from 21 million US accounts.
content: Character.AI is planning to sell millions of chat histories, says a group of state attorneys. Illustration by Algi Febri Sugita/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images State attorneys general move to block Character.AI from auctioning millions of private user chats. The objection says that datasets includes account details and sensitive chat histories. They said bankruptcy should not allow Character to sidestep federal and state privacy protections. A group of state attorneys general is asking a bankruptcy court to stop Character.AI from auctioning off millions of users’ private chatbot conversations, including records tied to children, to the highest bidder. In a filing on Tuesday, 42 state attorneys general said that the now- bankrupt AI chatbot company is planning to sell chat histories from 21 million US accounts, more than 2 million of which include children . the December 1 auction would also sell private information such as account details, IP addresses, and other metadata, as well as internal risk scores the company assigned users. The states argue that the terms of sale give users virtually no protection. A buyer would not be required to follow Character.AI’s privacy policy, honor deletion requests, or limit how it uses or resells the data, they said. The attorneys added that Character.AI had previously told users that it did not sell personal information for money. “Character.AI’s plan to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chat histories of its users — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling,” Bonta said in a statement. According to the states, the datasets include conversations involving self-harm, eating disorders, suicidal thoughts, sexual material and users who treated characters presenting themselves as therapists or doctors. The coalition asked the court to reject the terms of the sale, and the company’s proposed lead bidder, Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, an entity formed in Delaware a day before Character.AI selected it for the role. The states say bankruptcy should not allow Character.AI to sidestep federal and state privacy protections, particularly for children. At minimum, they said, any sale should exclude minors’ chats and other sensitive data and impose meaningful conditions on whoever acquires the company’s assets. Character.AI did not respond to a request for comment. Character.AI’s safety practices have faced intense scrutiny and multiple lawsuits. The company, its founders, and Google were sued by the mother of a Florida teenager who alleged that a chatbot fostered an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship with her 14-year-old son, reinforced his suicidal thoughts, and contributed to his death. Character.AI and Google later reached settlements in teen-harm lawsuits. The startup was founded by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas. In 2024, Google struck a roughly $2.7 billion deal for a nonexclusive license to Character.AI’s technology and brought the founders back to the company, while Character.AI continued operating independently. It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Young Americans are counting on stocks to build wealth. One economist says there's a catch that could kill this plan.
summary: Younger Americans' growing reliance on stocks to build wealth could limit the Fed's ability to tolerate a market downturn.
content: Younger Americans are increasingly dependent on stock-market performance to build wealth and fund their retirement. Spencer Platt/Getty Images Young Americans increasingly depend on stocks to build wealth as homeownership becomes harder to attain. An economist warns that historical equity returns point to a decade of zero returns. Millennials rely more on investment-based retirement plans than boomers, exposing them to market swings. Young Americans are increasingly dependent on the stock market to build wealth as traditional paths to financial security become harder to access. But one economist warns that historical market returns point to a potentially disappointing decade ahead. Steven Blitz, the chief US economist at GlobalData.TS Lombard, wrote on Wednesday that long-term equity-return data suggest investors should expect zero returns over the next 10 years. The warning comes as younger Americans face barriers to homeownership and savings deposits offer limited returns, leaving them increasingly reliant on equities to accumulate wealth for retirement, Blitz argued. "Households' feeling that the economy fails to deliver is rooted in reality not imagination," Blitz wrote. Millennials are particularly exposed because they rely more heavily on 401(k)-style retirement plans, whose value depends on investment performance, than traditional pensions. Blitz found that millennials have $1.30 in such retirement benefits for every dollar in traditional pension benefits, compared with $1.05 for Gen X and just 59 cents for baby boomers. Millennials also trail baby boomers in their asset-to-liability ratios at comparable life stages, though they are roughly on par with Generation X, according to the report. Blitz argues that the growing importance of equities to household finances has implications for monetary policy. The Federal Reserve traditionally influences economic activity through borrowing and lending costs, but household finances have become increasingly tied to equities rather than credit-driven spending, he said. That dependence could also constrain the Fed's ability to tolerate a sustained stock-market downturn, Blitz wrote, because falling share prices could undermine household wealth and confidence. "The economy is not broken, but it operates very differently, and policy has yet to adapt," Blitz wrote. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Storms disrupt Thanksgiving with flight delays, over 960,000 power outages, and a Delta ground stop at LaGuardia
summary: Over 960,000 households are without power on Thursday, and hundreds of flights have been canceled.
content: A storm is hitting the East Coast on Thanksgiving Day. Craig T Fruchtman/Getty Images Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel with flight delays and cancellations across the US. Over 960,000 households are without power on Thursday, and hundreds of flights have been canceled. Bad weather has led to the first-ever postponement of the Macy's Thanksgiving Parade. Storms are disrupting Thanksgiving travel and leading to power outages in homes across the East Coast. As of 8:30 p.m. ET Thursday, over 2,300 flights within, into, or out of the US had been delayed and 451 canceled, according to FlightAware. The day before, more than 6,500 flights were delayed and about 160 canceled. The National Weather Service wrote in a Wednesday report that the East Coast can expect "major coastal flooding, beach erosion, strong wind gusts, and heavy rainfall" during Thanksgiving. Scattered power outages and tree damage are also likely, it added. Over 960,000 US households were without power on Thursday evening, according to PowerOutage.us. That included about 124,000 in Virginia, 151,000 in Maryland, about 191,000 in New Jersey, and over 224,000 in Pennsylvania. A map from the weather service showed winter, gale, coastal flood, and wind warnings along the country's eastern coast. One in four flights departing Baltimore/Washington International were canceled, according to FlightAware. NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani wrote in a Wednesday X post that New Yorkers should expect severe weather on Thursday, including winds up to 60 miles per hour. On Thursday morning, LaGuardia Airport recorded wind gusts of up to 39 knots, or 45 miles per hour. Such strong winds can disrupt flying. LaGuardia issued a ground stop for aircraft from Delta Air Lines in the evening, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Mamdani said that, to protect New Yorkers, the city, along with Macy's and the local police department, had decided to postpone the 100th Annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday. This is the first time in history that the iconic parade has been rescheduled. "The worst of the storm is expected to hit on Thanksgiving Day in the afternoon through the late evening," he added in his X post. He provided a list of steps New Yorkers should take to protect themselves ahead of the storm, such as staying indoors, moving cars away from coastal areas to higher ground, and budgeting extra time for travel. The Transportation Security Administration said in a Saturday X post that it expects to screen nearly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between November 24 and November 30, including more than 3 million on Sunday, November 29. It recommended that travelers arrive early for their flights. The Federal Aviation Administration wrote in a Wednesday X post that gusty winds may slow flights at LaGuardia Airport, Newark Liberty Airport, JFK, and San Francisco International Airport that day. It added that thunderstorms may cause delays at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport. Disruption was worsened in Miami when a FedEx plane overshot the runway on Wednesday evening. No injuries were reported, though the incident caused inbound flights to be grounded for about 90 minutes. title: Who trusts influencers? These 4 stats reveal the state of creator marketing.
summary: Advertisers are spending billions on influencers. Here are key stats marketers need to know about Americans' attitudes toward creators.
content: Emma McIntyre/Getty Images for Sony Pictures Entertainment How do Americans really feel about influencers? Morning Consult surveyed about 2,000 US adults exclusively for Business Insider. Here are four stats influencer marketers should know — including who trusts influencers the most. Influencer marketing is ultimately powered by one thing: people's feelings. Whether you hit "buy" on an item an influencer is promoting could come down to how much you trust that creator. We wanted to get a gut-check on how Americans feel about influencers. Morning Consult conducted research exclusively for Business Insider and surveyed about 2,000 US adults in September about overall trust, purchase decisions and regrets, politics, and sponsorship disclosures. The biggest takeaway: Feelings about influencers — especially trust — vary greatly by income and generation. For instance, baby boomers often find influencers "annoying." Gen X, millennials, and Gen Z, on the other hand, say they feel "entertained" by them. A lot is at stake. Advertisers are expected to spend $44 billion on creators in the US in 2026, per the Interactive Advertising Bureau. Here are four key stats from Morning Consult's survey on influencers. 1. Higher-income social media users are more likely to trust influencers More money, more loyalty — when it comes to trusting influencers. According to Morning Consult's survey, 61% of high earners — those making over $100,000 — trust influencer product recommendations. These high earners are also more likely to be politically swayed by creators and want to become influencers themselves. For those earning less than $100,000, that trust fell to about 50%. In part, that's because higher earners can better relate to some creators' lifestyles, industry insiders said. Amanda Acevedo, director of talent at G&B Digital Management, told Business Insider that the "general population online knows creators make good money for themselves." Meanwhile, creators and marketers alike are tempering the luxury overload — like hauls or gift unboxings — as financial realities their followers face ebb and flow. "When you are making more money, you don't view them as out of touch because you can relate to it a bit more — you have more spending power," said Natalie Barbu, founder of Rella and a former lifestyle influencer. Read more 2. Only 31% of baby boomers 'at least somewhat' trust influencers There's a generational divide in attitudes toward influencers. Baby boomers (born between 1946 and 1964) are more distrustful of influencers compared to millennials (1981 to 1996) and Gen Z (1997 to 2012). According to Morning Consult's survey, 31% of boomers said they trust influencer recommendations at least somewhat, compared with 62% of Gen Z and 64% of millennials. Still, they aren't immune to influencer marketing, according to Lucy Kruszynski, global head of brand at influencer marketing agency Buttermilk. "Brands need to think about how creators can build credibility through consistent content over time," she told Business Insider. Read more 3. 69% of US adults think paid promos should be disclosed — but only 25% think influencers are actually doing so consistently Knowing that you are watching or seeing an ad is very important to US consumers. Influencers who don't disclose such details risk losing the trust of their audiences. Morning Consult found that 69% of US adults want to see disclosures on sponsored influencer content . However, only 25% actually believe influencers are disclosing these partnerships consistently. That perception might not be reality. A survey of content creators conducted by SheSpeaks found that 14% of creators said they didn't always disclose brand ties. According to the same SheSpeaks data, 18% of surveyed creators said that a brand had explicitly requested that they not disclose a partnership. Read more 4. Influencers aren't just driving purchases — 26% of US adults say influencers have swayed their votes Influencer content has the power to move the political dial. According to Morning Consult, about one in four US adults said that an influencer's content had affected who they'd voted for in an election. Younger Americans were more likely to be politically swayed by influencer content, too. Morning Consult found that three in four Gen Z respondents said influencers had shaped their views on political or social issues. Influencer marketing is a "big player in this space now," said Nicole Dunger, a founding partner at the marketing firm People First, which works with candidates and advocacy groups on their creator strategies. title: I pivoted from an architecture career to work at Sweetgreen. I have no regrets.
summary: Sweetgreen manager Bahareh Ghazaei studied architecture but found her calling in restaurants, where she helps workers move up.
content: Bahareh Ghazaei trained as an architect but prefers working with people in restaurants. Courtesy of Sweetgreen Bahareh Ghazaei studied architecture before pursuing a career in restaurant management. She said working in restaurants gives her more tangible results than her past work as a designer. Ghazaei loves seeing staff at a new store grow: "When they all start to run, that's amazing to watch." This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Bahareh Ghazaei, a general manager of restaurant chain Sweetgreen in Nashville. Ghazaei, 34, joined the company in 2021 after earning degrees in architecture and historic preservation. Business Insider verified her background. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity. I was born and raised in Iran. I moved to the States around 2020, to LA. I have my bachelor's in architecture and my master's in historic preservation. It was a bit difficult to enter the architecture market and design with no prior experience in the US. I found a part-time server job at a local restaurant. It was my first job in the industry. Soon, I became the head server. I also trained a couple of people, and I loved it. When you're training, you leave someone with a skill that they can use for the rest of their lives, no matter what they do. I eventually got a job at Sweetgreen as a shift manager. In nine months, I became an assistant coach, meaning assistant manager. Then, after about a year, I became the head coach, or general manager . After being in the role for about two years, I became a head coach-restaurateur for the company. They are the top head coaches. They're nominated by regional general managers and interviewed by Sweetgreen's CEO and COO. Less than a year after that, I moved to Nashville to open up our new market. The calm in the storm I love the human interaction. I think that's one of the reasons I didn't pursue architecture seriously here. I would be sitting at a computer all day. When you work with people, that's a living example of what you did. That's mind-blowingly amazing for me. What I achieve on a daily basis in restaurants is more tangible for me than what I can get as a designer. When you're in a position of manager or a shift manager, you get to impact a lot of lives. You directly impact your team's lives , but you indirectly impact your customers because a happy team will then give you a happy customer. At my prior stores, I had almost all my dishwashers becoming shift managers. That's something that I'm super proud of. I think about how I'm leaving these people. As long as I leave them better than how I found them, my job is done. That could even mean firing them because they're wasting their time here. That could be developing them. Two of my shift leaders back home in LA are now general managers. As a manager, you sometimes have to be the calm in the storm — or sometimes be the storm in the calm, depending on the situation. What I mean is we try to be ready before our peak happens. One of the biggest problems at Sweetgreen is your oven going down. When your oven is down, or you're cooking with one oven, you really need to unlock the "yes" mentality in your team. Don't say, "I don't have salmon." Say, "I'm out of salmon right now, but I have this, this, and this." Or, "Here's what I can do right now." That's a very stressful situation. You say to your team, "Let them know our oven is down. We're working on it. Here is an ETA, and thank you for your patience." When they start to run We opened the Nashville store in June. The job is not done until I see this store on the right track for success over the next three months. Sweetgreen grades restaurants periodically and quarterly. Success means getting an A. I don't want to say I'm a perfectionist, but I strive for excellence. With a new store in a new market, it's challenging to teach everybody at the same time. I think about about a day care where you have everybody in the crawling-to-standing-up stage. You have to hold this one; you have to grab that one. But at the end of the day, when they all start to run, that's amazing to watch. When I think about my career , I always want to do more. There are careers in our support center or our corporate office. I can work toward becoming an area manager or a district manager. There are different paths. That's something that's kept me going. title: 'A golden age for builders': Here's what business leaders are thankful for this year

content: Sam Altman, Fei-Fei Li, and Bill Ackman posted about what they were thankful for this Thanksgiving. Getty Images CEOs, VCs, and other business leaders are feeling reflective. Sam Altman said being a dad never gets old. Bill Ackman thanked the healthcare workers who have helped his daughter. Fei-Fei Li and Brian Armstrong took different approaches to expressing their gratitude. It's not just your neighbor or family friend firing off a Thanksgiving post. Business leaders can't seem to resist either. Sam Altman took the opportunity to reflect on fatherhood. "I am thankful for a lot of things in life, but my family is the best thing that has ever happened to me," the OpenAI CEO wrote on X. "Most good things get a little less satisfying the 100th time you do them," Altman added. She spent weeks in a coma and six months in the hospital. "Healthcare is a field, perhaps more so than any other, where people make a massive personal sacrifice of their lives, their time, their sleep, and their energy to help others," Ackman wrote on X. Investor and Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio, who has warned of a looming US debt crisis , emphasized the importance of connection amid turmoil in a post on LinkedIn. "I hope that we can keep in mind that despite all the challenges and conflicts in the world today, the most important thing is how we choose to be with each other," wrote Dalio. In a post on X, "Godmother of AI" Fei-Fei Li thanked the people in her life, including her students, colleagues, mentors, friends, and family, after noting that people often talk more about machines than each other. title: The vehicles that shaped Waymo's robotaxi fleet, from desert racers to luxury SUVs
summary: Waymo began as Google's secret Self-Driving Car project in 2008. Take a look at every vehicle that helped build its robotaxi fleet.
content: Waymo's robotaxis underwent multiple evolutions, including a concept for a Google-built car, before settling on electric SUVs. AP/Tony Avelar Waymo's operating robotaxi fleet is mainly made up of Jaguars and the Chinese-made Zeekrs. But did you know Waymo also designed a proprietary self-driving car with no steering wheel? Take a look at the different vehicle platforms Waymo explored before commercializing its service. Once upon a time, in Waymo's history , the Alphabet-backed robotaxi company designed its own autonomous car. Waymo, by now, is a 17-year-old project-turned-product that provides more than half a million fully autonomous rides a week and has started to expand beyond US roads. Its nearly two-decade legacy can be told through its pioneering figures, from Sebastian Thrun to Chris Urmson ; through its fierce rivalry with Cruise, Uber, and Tesla; through its evolution as a Google-backed business; or through its technology. Perhaps more vividly, though, the story of Waymo can be told through its cars. The Waymo robotaxi didn't immediately appear as the retrofitted Jaguar I-PACE most riders are familiar with today. Its earliest roots can be traced to a diesel-powered Volkswagen Touareg that competed in a desert race backed by the Department of Defense . As the company expands, Waymo has tapped companies abroad, including China's Zeekr and South Korea's Hyundai , to introduce newer vehicle platforms at lower costs. Take a look at all the cars that helped shape the robotaxi company. A 2004 Volkswagen Touareg retrofitted with a suite of sensors would get Google cofounder Larry Page's attention. Kim Kulish/Corbis via Getty Images In 2005, a Stanford University team led by Sebastian Thrun, pictured above, won the first-place, million-dollar prize in the DoD-backed Grand Challenge of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) for successfully building a car that can autonomously traverse 132 miles of Mojave Desert terrain. Volkswagen would provide Thrun's team with the base vehicle: a 2004 Volkswagen Touareg R5 TDI. The team would retrofit the car with five lasers, one camera, two radars, a GPS, and a six-processor Intel computer. The car was nicknamed Stanley, after the university. Stanley's victory caught the attention of Google cofounder Larry Page . Page would tap Thrun to lead what was then known as the Google Self-Driving Car project in 2008. A 2007 Chevrolet Tahoe showed that autonomous driving in urban environments was possible. David Paul Morris/Getty Images Two years after the Stanley victory, DARPA hosted another race. This time, the challenge required teams to navigate urban-like traffic rules and environments, including intersections, parking areas, and lane merging. A team from Carnegie Mellon University won first prize with a 2007 Chevrolet Tahoe named "Boss." The car was retrofitted with 13 lidars, 5 radars, and 2 cameras. Another key member of the Google Self-Driving Car Project emerged out of the race: Chris Urmson. Urmson acted as the project's chief technology officer before stepping into Thrun's role as the project leader in 2013. A modified 2008 Toyota Prius brought Google's self-driving dreams to real-world traffic environments. Karen Bleier/AFP via Getty Images The Toyota Prius made up Google's earliest real-world test fleet. The choice of the eco-friendly car could be traced to Anthony Levandowski, a technical lead in the Google project. In 2008, Levandowski, who by then had joined Google for its Streets project, and a team of Berkeley graduates built a self-driving Prius for a Discovery Channel series, "Prototype This!" The New Yorker reported. By 2009, Levandowski was brought in as a founding member of Google's autonomous driving project. The Prius would also become Google's first vehicle platform to receive an autonomous-vehicle testing license in Nevada. At the time, Nevada was the first state to create such a licensing regime for AVs. Google also had a brief taste for style with the Audi TT. Adrian Moser/Bloomberg via Getty Images Little's known about what was going through the minds of the folks at Google's self-driving project when they decided to include the Audi TT, a two-door luxury sports car, in its test fleet. The New York Times reported in 2010 that the project was using six Priuses and one Audi TT in its test fleet. A Waymo spokesperson told Business Insider that the TT was used as a support vehicle. The Lexus RX 450h was Google's first foray into self-driving SUVs. WASHINGTON, DC - APRIL 23: Googles Lexus RX 450H Self Driving Car is seen parked on Pennsylvania Ave. on April 23, 2014 in Washington, DC. Google has logged over 300,000 miles testing its self driving cars around the country. (Photo by Mark Wilson/Getty Images) Mark Wilson/Getty Images Urmson, in a 2012 blog post, said the hybrid Lexus was added to the test fleet to help the self-driving technology become familiar with "different environments and on different terrain." The New Yorker reported that the Lexus would be used for highway testing. The car also appeared to feature a sleeker and more compact sensor suite, Wired reported. Before the Tesla Cybercab, there was the Google Firefly. Scenes of daily life at Google X in Mountain View, California. A new Google self driving car is demonstrated for the media, elderly and legally blind test drivers at Google X in Mountain View, California. (Photo by Kim Kulish/Corbis via Getty Images) Kim Kulish/Corbis via Getty Images Google's Firefly was the company's vision for what self-driving vehicles should become: a car built for autonomy that removes the steering wheel, accelerator, and brake pedal. Press a button, and it will drive. The car was never meant to be commercialized, but more as a learning exercise, the company said. "By designing and building a truly self-driving vehicle from scratch, we were able to crack some of the earliest self-driving puzzles — where to place the sensors, how to integrate the computer, what controls passengers need in a car that drives itself," Waymo said in a blog post. The dome sensor on the roof of the Firefly would be the precursor to the now recognizable lidar hat on Waymo's current vehicle platforms. The company provided its first self-driving ride in a Firefly to a legally blind passenger, traversing some of Austin's roads. The 2017 Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid begins taking members of the public on autonomous rides. 07 May 2018, US, Mountain View: A self-driving car made by Google's sister company Waymo is on the road for a test drive. The car is a rebuilt minivan of the model Chrysler Pacifica by Fiat Chrysler. Photo: Andrej Sokolow/dpa (Photo by Andrej Sokolow/picture alliance via Getty Images) Andrej Sokolow/picture alliance via Getty Images In 2016, the Google Self-Driving Project announced a partnership with Fiat Chrysler Automobiles, which later became Stellantis, bringing Chrysler minivans to the robotaxi fleet. That same year, the project was spun out of Google and rebranded as Waymo. The car would see Waymo through its first early-rider program, which began in Phoenix in 2017, and through the first time the company opened its paid, fully driverless service to the public three years later. The Chrysler ran on Waymo's fourth-generation autonomous driving system. It had 6 lidars, 6 radars, and 19 cameras, a Waymo spokesperson said. Waymo retired the Chrysler in May 2023, giving the minivan a seven-year run. The Jaguar I-PACE scales Waymo's commercial robotaxi business. Two Waymo self-driving Jaguar robotaxies drive on Tower Bridge Road, on 11th September 2026, in London, England. Waymo are testing their vehicles around the capital using a driver at the wheel. Waymo say they're not yet offering commercial rides, but instead testing 24/7 to ensure their technology can safely handle all of London's road conditions. From September 3rd, self-driving cars have been available for hire in central London. (Photo by Richard Baker / In Pictures via Getty Images) Richard Baker/In Pictures via Getty Images The Chrysler helped jump-start the Waymo brand, but the Jaguar I-PACE, an all-electric SUV, would turn the company into a multi-city business. Waymo introduced the white Jaguars to the fleet in 2018. The cars quickly became a fixture of San Francisco roads even before Waymo began its paid service in the city in 2023. The car also introduced Waymo's fifth-generation driver, stacked with 29 cameras, 5 lidars, and 6 radars. Today, the Jaguar remains Waymo's main workhorse, making up the majority of the more than 4,000 robotaxis active across 15 metro regions in the US. The Chinese-made Zeekr CM1e introduces the cheaper, next-generation Waymo driver. Venice Beach, CA - May 27, 2026: Waymo's new autonomous vehicle, called the Ojai, drives in Venice Beach on Wednesday, May 27, 2026. The all-electric vehicle, equipped with the company's sixth-generation autonomous driving system, is expected to begin limited rides with select customers in Los Angeles, San Francisco and Phoenix in the coming weeks. (Allen J. Schaben / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) The news is under embargo until May 28th at 8am. Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images With plans to go international and expand its robotaxi business, Waymo introduced a new vehicle platform that it said costs a fraction of what the Jaguar I-PACE costs. The vehicle is from Zeekr, a Chinese EV company, but Waymo rebranded the cars as Ojai. The car also came with the sixth-generation Waymo Driver, which includes a reduced sensor suite: 13 cameras, 4 lidars, and 6 radars. Waymo hasn't specified how much cheaper the Ojais are. The company has said that, in addition to lower vehicle costs, the Ojai is easier to clean and maintain. Business Insider reported during its ride test that the Ojai has more passenger room, more luggage space, and easier entry. The Hyundai Ioniq 5 will continue Waymo's expansion plans. LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 21: Waymo’s sixth-generation fully autonomous technology – the Waymo Driver – is outfitted on Hyundai’s all-electric IONIQ 5 SUV, which will be added to the Waymo One fleet over time, is on display during the Los Angeles Auto Show at the Los Angeles Convention Center on November 21, 2025 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Josh Lefkowitz/Getty Images) Josh Lefkowitz/Getty Images The Ioniq 5 , made by South Korea's Hyundai, is another extension of Waymo's ongoing expansion plans that's being tested on public roads. It'll come equipped with Waymo's sixth-generation driver. Both the Ojai and the Hyundai will make up Waymo's robotaxi fleet of the future, as the company eventually phases out the Jaguars. Semafor reported on Monday that Waymo has plans to increase its robotaxi fleet to 8,000 by the end of the year and to 20,000 by the end of 2027, citing people familiar with the matter. A Waymo spokesperson said it aims to roll out the Hyundai to the public sometime next year Read the original article on Business Insider

title: An exec wanted to better understand entrepreneurs, so he launched a candle company from his kitchen. Here's what he learned.
summary: The side-hustle experiment taught Ian Watson that making a product can be easier than navigating the paperwork required to sell it.
content: Ian Watson and his husband, Iain Cumming, started The Meltdown from their Palm Springs kitchen. Courtesy of Ian Watson Ian Watson started a side hustle to better understand entrepreneurs. He and his husband launched a cheekily branded candle business, selling scents like 'Sunday Panic' and 'FML.' Making the product was the easy part. Navigating permits and compliance took longer than anticipated. Ian Watson spends his workdays helping small businesses navigate payroll, benefits, and the other logistical realities of running a company. As Gusto 's chief customer officer, he wanted a more complete understanding of what it's actually like to start a business. It's a habit he's developed throughout his career in customer experience. While working at Qantas, he understood the frustration of delayed bags and disrupted trips as a traveler. At Airbnb, where he worked before Gusto, he became a host to better understand the anxiety of welcoming strangers into his home. Empathizing with entrepreneurs was a new challenge, Watson said, because he had never run a business himself. So he and his husband, Iain Cumming, started The Meltdown, a cheekily branded candle business selling highly relatable scents, from "Sunday Panic" and "Shady Pines" to "Gin & Regret" and "FML." They bought wax and fragrances, turned weekends into candle-testing sessions, and ran roughly 150 potential product names past friends and colleagues. The Palm Springs-based side hustle has already taught Watson two valuable lessons about entrepreneurship. 1. Making the product was easier than he expected Neither Watson nor his husband had made a candle before. They began with a basic kit designed to make six candles at home, then spent three months experimenting with scents, wax, branding, and packaging. "It was a lot of playing around and doing research to start with," Watson told Business Insider — both in terms of making the candles and developing the brand. The candle-making itself was "like mixology," he said. After experimenting with different scents, they gifted early versions to friends. Watson and Cumming started selling their candles at a local night market in Palm Springs. Courtesy of The Meltdown For the branding, they looked at the candle companies that resonated with them, those that didn't, and the gap they could fill. Much of the branding they encountered was rooted in health and wellness, Watson said, "but none of them are honest about what the real issue is — about why you're lighting a candle." Their answer was to build a brand around the messier realities their customers might actually be trying to escape. They went for "big and bold," he said, rather than discreet. View this post on Instagram A post shared by themeltdownps (@themeltdownps) So far, that strategy appears to be working. Once they mastered small-batch production, they used Claude to figure out how to scale while maintaining consistency. They launched at a weekly Palm Springs night market, where they found early customers and drew interest from local businesses looking to carry the candles wholesale. Next, they're focused on building a website to support online sales. "The actual making of a product is a lot easier than you think," Watson said. "If you've got an idea and something that you're passionate about, go do it." 2. Getting permission to sell the product was much harder Watson expected the business to be ready for its first market within about four weeks. Instead, it took closer to three months. Before selling a single candle, the couple had to register an LLC, secure seller's permits in California and Riverside County, shop for liability insurance, and pitch a farmers market review board for a spot. The Meltdown candles are hand-poured in Palm Springs. Courtesy of The Meltdown They also had to complete the required steps to use their business name. In California, that meant paying to publish it in a newspaper for four consecutive weeks while waiting to see whether anyone objected. "The fact that it takes a month before we can confirm that we can use that name — it's such an old, antiquated process," Watson said. "No one's looking at a newspaper anymore. That blew my mind." The experience gave Watson a sharper view of the pressures facing the entrepreneurs Gusto serves. The product may be the fun part, but the paperwork, compliance requirements, and costs can arrive long before the first sale. The couple's goal is to turn The Meltdown into a profitable business that can pay Cumming a salary. For now, their eight-year-old kid has one particularly fragrant bedroom: It doubles as their warehouse, with roughly 1,000 candles stacked on shelves. "It is the best-smelling eight-year-old bedroom in the world," Watson said. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: I've flown to 14 countries with my cat. From airline rules to etiquette, here are 5 mistakes pet owners make when flying.
summary: Flying with a pet means following airline and country rules and avoiding habits that can derail your trip or annoy other passengers.
content: I travel full-time with my cat and have mastered the complexities of flying with her. Harrison Pierce I've spent the past five years traveling around the world with my cat, Isabelle. Through a lot of trial and error, we've almost perfected pet travel. I often see people let untrained pets out of carriers or misunderstand country entry rules. About five years ago, I sold almost everything I owned, bought a one-way ticket to Italy, and brought my four-year-old cat, Isabelle, along for the journey. Since then, we've flown thousands of miles on dozens of flights to 14 countries and counting across North America, South America, and Europe. Through trial and error — including mistakes that cost me thousands of dollars — we've turned pet travel into a science. Flying with a pet means following airline and country rules — and avoiding annoying habits that can inconvenience other passengers or derail a trip. Here are 5 things pet owners can get wrong at the airport. Letting your pet out of the carrier Isabelle fits in a pet carrier under the seat. Harrison Pierce Although you see pets on leashes all the time on social media, airline policies generally require pets to remain inside their carriers throughout the travel journey, including at the airport, in the lounge, on the plane, and upon landing. Service animals are subject to different rules. Still, I'm constantly seeing videos of cats asleep on airplane seats or perched on people's shoulders as they walk through the airport. It's cute and might make for viral content , but it can create a problem for everyone around you. Even if your pet is well-trained at home, an airport or airplane is an unfamiliar and stressful environment. Outside their carrier, a pet could escape, bother another traveler, trigger someone's allergies, or cause damage. I travel full-time with Isabelle, so the last thing I want is trouble with an airline or a pet escaping in a busy airport. I'm also aware that not every fellow passenger wants a cat crawling into their lap. Not preparing your pet for a long travel day The expandable cat carrier. Harrison Pierce When it's time to travel, I use a backpack-style carrier so I can keep my hands free. It's expandable, so when we're in a lounge, I can give Isabelle a little more room to move around. I pack her supplies in the carrier pockets and put the same blanket inside each time we fly so she has a familiar place to curl up. I find that familiar smells and routines help her settle into travel mode. I also make sure every opening on the carrier is fully secured before boarding. I've heard plenty of stories about owners not closing a carrier all the way and a pet slipping out at the airport or on the plane. I don't sedate Isabelle for flights. Sedation can pose health risks for pets during air travel, so I stick to natural calming treats. Waiting too long to add your pet to a flight Flights can only accommodate a small number of pets. Al Drago/Getty Images Most airlines limit the number of pets allowed in the cabin, so I book early and add Isabelle to my reservation as soon as I can. If you wait until close to departure or at check-in, the airline may already have reached its pet limit. Then, you may have to change flights and potentially pay a fee, depending on the fare you booked. Airlines can also have specific pet restrictions by route and destination. For example, most US airlines don't allow pets in the cabin on flights to or from Colombia. When I take Isabelle there, I fly a US airline from North Carolina to Miami and book a separate flight from Miami to Colombia on Colombian flag carrier Avianca. It adds another step to planning — and a connection that would solely be on the traveler to not miss — but it's much better than finding out your pet can't board after you've already booked a nonrefundable ticket. Not telling security you have a pet Security is the toughest part of the travel day. Al Drago/Getty Images Security is usually the most stressful part of the travel day, especially when I'm in a country where I don't speak the language. You generally need to remove your pet from the carrier and send the carrier through the X-ray machine. Then, you carry your pet through a metal detector before putting them back in the carrier. For Isabelle's first year of travel , I put her in a harness and leash before security in case she got scared and tried to run. We have a great routine now, and she usually sits calmly in my arms, so I no longer use a harness that could make her uncomfortable. I always tell security staff upfront that I have a pet. You can't go through a full-body scanner while holding an animal, and mentioning it early can save you the hassle of switching lanes. Not checking the entry rules and paperwork Isabelle has a passport. Harrison Pierce Before I book any flight, I check the destination's animal-import rules, including quarantine requirements, vaccinations, required tests, airline restrictions, and paperwork. Depending on the destination, that can mean getting a vet certificate shortly before travel and having it endorsed by a government agency before departure. When we arrive, officials review the paperwork and may charge an entry fee. Argentina, for example, didn't charge us anything, while other destinations have charged a nominal fee, often around $25. I avoid places that require long quarantines. I was considering a trip to Australia, but pets entering there from many countries may be subject to quarantine lasting 10 to 30 days. Since I usually stay in one place for only two or three months, that doesn't make sense for us. Isabelle travels everywhere with me. Harrison Pierce I've learned the importance of researching the required tests before booking flights the hard way. When I planned a trip to Peru, I didn't realize Isabelle needed a rabies titer test to enter from Europe, and I couldn't get it done in time. Instead, I had to make a last-minute detour to North Carolina to leave her with my parents for a couple of months. Luckily, I'd booked my original flight with miles, so it was refundable. Still, the detour added thousands of miles of flying, cost a couple hundred dollars in new tickets, and I couldn't cancel the nonrefundable, pet-friendly Airbnbs — which are often more expensive — that I no longer needed. The key is reviewing everything yourself. Not every vet regularly completes international pet health certificates, and a missing field, an incorrect date, or another small mistake can mean starting over, or being turned away at the border. title: YouTube wants more paid users. Exclusive content like a new K-pop documentary could help.
summary: YouTube just released an exclusive film featuring Blackpink's Lisa, and it could signal a new playbook for differentiating itself from Netflix.
content: Lalisa Manobal (Lisa) at the premiere of "Always Lalisa," which is now exclusively available to YouTube Premium subscribers. Robin Marchant/Getty Images YouTube just released an exclusive documentary starring Blackpink's Lisa for its paid subscribers. Exclusives could be a useful marketing tool for YouTube as it aims to grow its Premium service. It could also help differentiate its paid offering as Netflix and others embrace creator content. YouTube wants to lure more users to its paid subscription offering, Premium. Will exclusive content help drive sign-ups? Last week, the company rolled out a Premium-only documentary featuring Lalisa Manobal, or Lisa, a solo artist and member of the K-pop group Blackpink. The Sony Music Vision film, "Always Lalisa," premiered in September at the Toronto International Film Festival and briefly showed up on Imax screens before landing on YouTube. YouTube hasn't publicly shared view counts for "Always Lalisa," but the trailer for the documentary drew 245 million views, suggesting it had wide appeal. Exclusive content isn't really part of YouTube's pitch for Premium, which focuses on ad-free videos, downloads, and background listening. But as competitors like Netflix begin to move onto its turf, adding content from YouTubers like Salish Matter and The Stokes Twins to its catalog alongside originals like "Stranger Things," the video app may need to respond in kind. Other streamers have successfully leveraged exclusives to score new sign-ups. In 2020, on the weekend that Disney Plus added the Broadway show "Hamilton" to its platform, it experienced a 7.4x spike in US sign-ups compared to the previous four weekends, according to estimates from the media analytics company Antenna. Peacock gained 2.8 million new subscribers during the first week of the 2024 Paris Olympics , which its owner NBC Universal broadcast exclusively in the US. YouTube could similarly drive some new Premium sign-ups if it can lock down exclusive content that matches the tastes of prospective subscribers using the data it already has on its more than 2 billion monthly active users, said Monica Khan, a former YouTube staffer who now runs an advisory firm for creators and brands called Creator Revolution. "Knowing my experience working at YouTube, everything is data-driven," Khan said. "YouTube should and will continue to selectively invest in exclusive creator programming when there is a compelling business case," she said. The company should use data to identify programming opportunities where there's "established fandom," she added. YouTube doesn't need to mess around with full-scale original productions like it did in the past, with mixed results. It produced shows like the karate drama "Cobra Kai" via its YouTube Red and YouTube Originals initiatives, but sunset its Originals program in 2022. YouTube Premium is an increasingly important revenue stream for the video app. While YouTube's ad revenue growth slowed in the third quarter, it said its subscriptions business is growing faster than ads. The company in October said it had over 150 million YouTube Music and Premium subscribers, up from 125 million in March 2025. YouTube charges less than Netflix for its service. Its ad-free offering is $15.99 a month (or $8.99 for Premium Lite, a lower cost version that includes ads on YouTube Music), while Netflix starts at $19.99 a month.
